key: COMP.DIG.L08.02|When you turn off a filter, what happens to the hidden rows? They show again, they are gone forever, or they move to a new sheet?
COMP.DIG.L08.02|What does sort do? Puts rows in order by a column, adds up all the numbers in a column, or hides the rows that do not match?
COMP.DIG.L08.02|In the strainer idea, what stays in the bowl? The rows that match, or every row?
how: A new way: a filter is like a strainer for pasta. The water goes through, and only what you want stays in the bowl.

key: COMP.DIG.L08.02|Sort 4, 9 and 6 largest first. Which comes first? 9, or 4?
how: A simpler step: sort three numbers largest first.

key: COMP.DIG.L08.02|What is =SUM of 45 and 60? 105, or 15?
how: The skill underneath: Spreadsheet Formulas (Computing Level 7). After sorting or filtering, formulas like =MAX and =SUM still work on the numbers.

key: COMP.DIG.L08.03|Look at the code. What is CAT shifted forward by 1? DBU, BZS, or CAT?
how: A simple code shifts each letter forward in the alphabet. Shift by 1: A becomes B, B becomes C, and so on.
pic: Shift each letter forward by 1:\nC A T

key: COMP.DIG.L08.03|What does the lock icon next to a web address mean? The site scrambles what you send, the site is closed for the day, or the site is slow to load?
how: A lock icon next to a web address means the site uses encryption, so others cannot read what you send.
pic: 🔒 https://

key: COMP.DIG.L08.03|Look at the code. What is ABC shifted forward by 2? CDE, BCD, or ABC?
pic: Shift each letter forward by 2:\nA B C

key: COMP.DIG.L08.03|Look at the code. What is the hidden word? HELLO, JGNNQ, or IFMMP?
pic: Shift each letter back by 1:\nI F M M P

key: COMP.DIG.L08.03|What is two-step sign-in? A password plus a code sent to your phone, two passwords written on paper, or signing in twice by mistake?
COMP.DIG.L08.03|Why is the key so important in encryption? Without it the message stays scrambled, keys make the message colorful, or keys are not really needed?
COMP.DIG.L08.03|Put the steps in order to send a coded message. The cards say: Your friend shifts it back with the key., Write the message., Shift each letter with the key.
COMP.DIG.L08.03|Abba enters his credit card on a store website. Which sign shows the page is encrypted? A lock icon next to the address, a bright sale banner, or many pictures of the items?
COMP.DIG.L08.03|Look at the code. What is DOG shifted forward by 3? GRJ, ELH, or DOG?
pic: Shift each letter forward by 3:\nD O G

key: COMP.DIG.L08.03|In the box idea, who can read the message? The person with the key, or anyone who carries the box?
how: A new way: encryption is like a locked box. Anyone can carry the box, but only the person with the key can open it.

key: COMP.DIG.L08.03|Shift the letter B forward by 1. What do you get? C, or A?
how: A simpler step: one letter. Shift A forward by 1 and it becomes B.

key: COMP.DIG.L08.03|Which password is a better key? Lulav!Sky7Bright, or abc?
how: The skill underneath: Strong Passwords (Computing Level 5). A password is a key, so it must be long, mixed and secret.

key: COMP.TYPE.L09.01|What does a typing certificate show? That you type fast and correctly, that you own a computer, or that you can type in many colors and fonts?
how: A typing certificate shows that you can type fast and correctly, like a grown-up at work. You take a timed test: type a passage for a few minutes, then count your speed and accuracy. Good posture and a steady rhythm win, not rushing. Let's earn that certificate!

key: COMP.TYPE.L09.01|Moshe typed 200 words in 5 minutes. What is his speed in words per minute? 40, 195, or 1000?
how: Speed is words per minute: divide the words you typed by the minutes.

key: COMP.TYPE.L09.01|Dovid typed 20 words and 18 were correct. What is his accuracy? 90 percent, 18 percent, or 2 percent?
how: Accuracy is the part you typed correctly. 45 correct out of 50 words is 90 percent.

key: COMP.TYPE.L09.01|Eli typed 150 words in 3 minutes. What is his speed? 50, 147, or 450?
COMP.TYPE.L09.01|Yossi typed 40 words and 30 were correct. What is his accuracy? 75 percent, 30 percent, or 10 percent?
COMP.TYPE.L09.01|Which posture is best for a long typing test? Sit tall with feet flat, slouch low in the chair, or rest your wrists on the desk edge?
COMP.TYPE.L09.01|During the test you make a mistake. What is the smart thing to do? Fix it quickly and keep going, stop the test and start over, or look down at the keys for a while?
COMP.TYPE.L09.01|Put the steps of a typing test in order. The cards say: Count speed and accuracy., Sit tall with fingers on home row., Type the passage for the timed minutes.
COMP.TYPE.L09.01|Chaim is typing the notes from the shul meeting, about 300 words. He types 30 words a minute. How many minutes will it take? 10, 270, or 9000?
COMP.TYPE.L09.01|Mendy typed 240 words in 6 minutes. What is his speed? 40, 234, or 1440?
COMP.TYPE.L09.01|Zevi typed 50 words and 40 were correct. What is his accuracy? 80 percent, 40 percent, or 10 percent?
COMP.TYPE.L09.01|Why does accuracy matter as much as speed? Mistakes must be fixed, which costs time; speed is all that counts; or accuracy is only for art class?
COMP.TYPE.L09.01|In the race idea, what is like a typing mistake? Falling down, or running steady?
how: A new way: typing is like running a race. Running fast but falling down slows you more than running steady.

key: COMP.TYPE.L09.01|40 words in 2 minutes. What is the speed? 20, or 42?
how: A simpler step: divide. 60 words in 2 minutes is 30 words a minute.

key: COMP.TYPE.L09.01|Which keys type an exclamation mark? Shift + 1, or Shift + 5?
how: The skill underneath: Numbers and Symbols (Computing Level 8). Timed tests include numbers and symbols, so the top row must be fast too.

key: COMP.PROG.L09.01|Look at the program. How many sides does it draw? 3, 4, or 90?
how: Look at this program. The goal is a square, which has 4 sides. Count how many sides the program really draws.
pic:
Goal: draw a square
repeat 3
  move 50
  turn 90

key: COMP.PROG.L09.01|Why fix only one thing at a time? So you know which change worked, because it is faster to type, or so the program is shorter?
how: Fix one thing at a time, then test. If you change many things at once, you will not know which change fixed it.

key: COMP.PROG.L09.01|Look at the program. What is the fix? Change repeat 3 to repeat 4, change move 50 to move 90, or delete turn 90?
pic:
Goal: draw a square
repeat 3
  move 50
  turn 90

key: COMP.PROG.L09.01|Look at the program. Which numbers does it say? 1 to 4, 1 to 5, or 2 to 5?
pic:
Goal: say 1 to 5
set n to 1
repeat until n = 5
  say n
  change n by 1

key: COMP.PROG.L09.01|Look at the program again. What is the bug? It stops before saying 5, it says 6 right after 5, or it never stops counting up?
pic:
Goal: say 1 to 5
set n to 1
repeat until n = 5
  say n
  change n by 1

key: COMP.PROG.L09.01|Mendy's game character walks through walls. Where should he look first? The blocks that handle walls, the title screen at the start, or the music that plays in the game?
COMP.PROG.L09.01|Put the debugging steps in order. The cards say: Test it again., Find the first step that goes wrong., Say what should happen., Fix that one step.
COMP.PROG.L09.01|Look at the program. What is the bug? Change score by -1 should be change score by 1, answer = 7 should be answer = 8, or there is no bug?
pic: Goal: add 1 to the score for a right answer\nif answer = 7\n  then change score by -1

key: COMP.PROG.L09.01|What is a bug? A mistake in a program, an insect inside the computer, or a fast program?
COMP.PROG.L09.01|After you fix a bug, what should you do? Test it again, never run it, or delete the fix?
COMP.PROG.L09.01|In the lights idea, what is the bad bulb? The bug, or the whole program?
how: A new way: debugging is like finding which bulb is out in a string of lights. You check one bulb at a time until you find the bad one.

key: COMP.PROG.L09.01|Goal: clap 3 times. The program claps 2 times. Is there a bug? Yes, or no?
how: A simpler step: just compare. The goal says 3 claps. The program claps 2 times.

key: COMP.PROG.L09.01|Which helps you find a bug fastest? A clear goal sentence, or no plan at all?
how: The skill underneath: Plan Before You Code (Computing Level 6). A clear goal from your plan tells you what should happen, so you can spot what went wrong.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.01|What is a budget? A plan for money coming in and going out, a kind of bank where you keep your savings, or a shopping list and nothing else?
how: A budget is a plan for your money: what comes in, what goes out, and what is left. A spreadsheet makes budgets easy, because =SUM adds each column and one simple formula shows what is left. Businesses, families and yeshivos all run on budgets. Let's build one!

key: COMP.DIG.L09.01|Look at the sheet. What will cell B5 show? 120, 90, or 50?
how: =SUM(B2:B4) adds all the money in column B, from row 2 to row 4.

Bar mitzvah savings

 1 │ Item     │ Dollars
 2 │ Birthday │ 50
 3 │ Chores   │ 30
 4 │ Tutoring │ 40
 5 │ Total    │ =SUM(B2:B4)

key: COMP.DIG.L09.01|Money in is 60 and money out is 52. What is the balance? 8, 112, or 52?
how: The balance is what is left: total money in minus total money out. A balance below 0 means you spent more than you had.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.01|Look at the sheet. What is the total income? 60, 52, or 20?
pic:
Monthly plan

key: COMP.DIG.L09.01|A family's balance is -20. What does that mean? They spent 20 more than they had, they saved 20 extra dollars, or nothing at all happened to their money that month?
COMP.DIG.L09.01|Why use a spreadsheet for a budget instead of paper? Formulas update when numbers change, paper cannot hold any numbers, or spreadsheets make you spend less?
COMP.DIG.L09.01|In the cup idea, what is the water left in the cup? The balance, or the spending?
how: A new way: a budget is like a cup of water. Income pours in, spending pours out, and the balance is what stays in the cup.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.01|15 dollars in, 9 spent. What is left? 6, or 24?
how: A simpler step: two numbers. 10 dollars in, 4 dollars spent, 6 left.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.01|What is =SUM of 15, 25 and 10? 50, or 40?
how: The skill underneath: Spreadsheet Formulas (Computing Level 7). =SUM, =MAX and the others work the same in a budget.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.02|How does an AI program learn? From patterns in many examples, by going to school like a boy, or by reading your mind somehow?
how: AI, short for artificial intelligence, is a computer program that learns patterns from huge numbers of examples. That lets it sort pictures, suggest words or answer questions. But AI predicts what is likely; it does not truly understand, and it can be wrong. Let's learn what it does and how to use it wisely!

key: COMP.DIG.L09.02|An AI saw thousands of pictures labeled apple. What has it learned? What apples usually look like, how apples taste when ripe, or how to grow apples in a garden?
how: To teach an AI to spot apples, people show it many pictures labeled apple and not apple. It learns what apples usually look like.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.02|An AI gives a confident answer. What should you do? Check it in a trusted source, believe it because it sounds sure, or share it with everyone right away?
how: AI predicts the most likely answer. Most of the time that helps, but sometimes it makes up something that sounds right and is wrong.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.02|Which job does AI do well? Sorting thousands of photos fast, knowing what you feel inside, or deciding what is right for you and your family?
COMP.DIG.L09.02|Why can an AI be wrong? It predicts and can guess badly, it never runs on a computer, or it only works late at night?
COMP.DIG.L09.02|An AI chat asks for your home address. What do you do? Do not share it and tell a grown-up, type it in so it can help, or share your password as well so it can log in?
COMP.DIG.L09.02|An AI learned only from pictures of red apples. What might it get wrong? It may not spot green apples, it will know every fruit, or nothing can go wrong at all?
COMP.DIG.L09.02|Put the steps in order to teach an AI to spot cats. The cards say: Test it on new pictures., Gather many labeled pictures., Let it learn the patterns.

COMP.DIG.L09.02|Dovid asks an AI for the date of a Yom Tov this year. What should he do with the answer? Check it in a Jewish calendar, trust it with no check at all, or ask again until the answers agree?
COMP.DIG.L09.02|What does AI stand for? Artificial intelligence, automatic internet, or always informed?
COMP.DIG.L09.02|An AI writes a report with a fact you cannot find anywhere else. What is likely? The AI may have made it up, it is surely true, or the internet is broken?
COMP.DIG.L09.02|Who is responsible for work you hand in, even if an AI helped? You are, the AI is, or nobody is?
COMP.DIG.L09.02|In the guesser idea, what is the AI doing? Making a smart guess, or knowing for sure?
how: A new way: AI is like a very fast guesser who has seen millions of examples. It guesses well, but it is still guessing.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.02|Which AI will spot dogs better? One shown 1000 dog pictures, or one shown 10?
how: A simpler step: more examples help. An AI shown many pictures learns better than one shown only a few.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.02|An AI answer has no source listed. Is it safe to trust it without checking? No, or yes?
how: The skill underneath: Judge a Source (Computing Level 6). An AI answer is a source too: ask who made it, and check it somewhere else.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.03|How do most jobs today use computers? To keep records, plan and talk to people; only for playing games at lunch; or not at all, since paper is better?
how: Almost every job uses computers: doctors keep records, builders draw plans, store owners track sales, and teachers make lessons. Knowing the right tool, writing clear emails and keeping files organized will help you in any job. Let's see computing at work!

key: COMP.DIG.L09.03|A store owner wants to add up a week of sales. Which tool fits best? A spreadsheet, a slide show, or a drawing app?
how: Pick the right tool: a document for writing, a spreadsheet for numbers, slides for presenting.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.03|Which is the best subject line for a work email about tomorrow's meeting? Meeting tomorrow at 10, hi, or urgent read now?
how: A work email needs a clear subject, a polite greeting, short sentences and your name at the end.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.03|Which file name helps coworkers find a file later? Budget-March-2026, my file final final, or new document 7 copy?
COMP.DIG.L09.03|A teacher wants to show a lesson to the whole class on the board. Which tool fits best? Slides, a spreadsheet, or a calculator?
COMP.DIG.L09.03|How should a work email to the principal begin? Dear Rabbi Cohen; hey dude; or no greeting at all?
COMP.DIG.L09.03|Why should workers back up important files? So work is not lost if a computer breaks, to make the computer run faster, or to delete all the old files from the computer for good?
COMP.DIG.L09.03|Put the steps in order to send a work email. The cards say: Read it over and send., Write a clear subject., Write a short and polite message.

COMP.DIG.L09.03|Abba runs a small store and wants to know which item sold the most this month. Which computer skill helps most? Sorting sales in a spreadsheet, drawing a poster for the store, or typing a story about the store?
COMP.DIG.L09.03|Which tool is best for writing a letter to a customer? A document, a spreadsheet, or a calculator?
COMP.DIG.L09.03|What should never go in a shared work file? Private passwords, the company's reports, or work emails to customers?
COMP.DIG.L09.03|Which is a clear work email sentence? The meeting is moved to 3:00 on Tuesday; meeting moved to sometime next week idk; or lol see u whenever the meeting is?
COMP.DIG.L09.03|In the toolbox idea, what is a spreadsheet like? The tool made for numbers, or the tool for words?
how: A new way: computer tools are like tools in a toolbox. A hammer for nails, a saw for wood; a spreadsheet for numbers, a document for words.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.03|You need to add 30 prices. Which tool? A spreadsheet, or slides?
how: A simpler step: one choice. Numbers go in a spreadsheet.

key: COMP.DIG.L09.03|What should be bigger than the body text in a work document? A heading, or a footnote?
how: The skill underneath: Professional Documents (Computing Level 8). Work writing uses the same headings, lists and neat fonts.

key: COMP.PROG.L09.02|What is a capstone program? A big project that uses all your skills, the very first program you ever write, or a program written with no plan or tests at all?
how: A capstone is the big project that shows everything you have learned. You plan a program, build it with variables, if, loops and functions, trace it line by line, and test it until it works. This is how real programmers work every day. Let's build your capstone!

key: COMP.PROG.L09.02|Look at the program. What does the total program print? 20, 5, or 9?
how: Trace the loop: total starts at 0 and adds 5 each time the loop runs.

total = 0
for i in range(4):
  total = total + 5
print(total)

key: COMP.PROG.L09.02|Look at the program. What does the double program print? 14, 7, or 72?
how: A function with return sends an answer back. double(7) puts 7 in for n.

key: COMP.PROG.L09.02|Before writing a big program, what should you do first? Write the goal and plan the steps, type as fast as you can, or skip testing to save time?

COMP.PROG.L09.02|Your capstone gives the wrong answer for one test. What do you do? Find the first wrong step and fix it, delete the whole program and quit, or ignore that one test and move on to the next part?
COMP.PROG.L09.02|Why use a function in a capstone? To reuse a job without retyping it, to make the program longer, or to hide the bugs from testers?
COMP.PROG.L09.02|In the sukkah idea, what is checking that it is sturdy? Testing, or planning?
how: A new way: a capstone is like building a sukkah. You plan it, put up each wall, check it is sturdy, and fix what wobbles.

key: COMP.PROG.L09.02|x = 2, then x = x + 3. What is x? 5, or 3?
how: A simpler step: trace one line. x = 4 and then x = x + 1 makes x equal 5.

key: COMP.PROG.L09.02|Goal: print 10. The program prints 9. Is there a bug? Yes, or no?
how: The skill underneath: Debugging and Testing (Computing Level 9). A capstone is only finished when every test passes.

key: COMP.TYPE.L10.01|What is the goal for this level? 35 words a minute at 90 right out of 100, 60 words a minute at 80 right out of 100, or 40 words a minute at 95 right out of 100?
how: You earned your Typing Certificate at 35 words a minute. Now we build real high-school speed: 40 words a minute, with 95 of every 100 words right, for a full 5 minutes. At that speed a two-page essay takes you minutes, not an evening, and your thoughts reach the page as fast as you think them.

key: COMP.TYPE.L10.01|Look at the test. How many words per minute is it? 50, 200, or 40?
how: Over 5 minutes you must keep your speed steady. Count your words: every 5 letters or spaces is one word. Then share them over the minutes. 1,000 letters and spaces in 5 minutes is 200 words, and 200 ÷ 5 = 40 words a minute.
pic: Typing test: 5 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 1000\nWords with a mistake: 10 of 200

key: COMP.TYPE.L10.01|Look at the test. How many out of every 100 words were right? 98, 95, or 90?
how: Watch how a typist checks accuracy. He typed 200 words and 10 had a mistake. Right words: 200 − 10 = 190. 190 ÷ 200 = 0.95, which is 95 out of 100. He passes this level, just barely!

COMP.TYPE.L10.01|What wins a 5-minute typing test? A fast start, a steady pace, or many short bursts?
how: A new way: think of a long-distance runner. He does not sprint and then stop; he keeps one steady pace for the whole race. Typing 5 minutes is the same: a steady pace beats a fast start.

key: COMP.TYPE.L10.01|In the simpler step, how long is the first run? 10 minutes, 1 minute, or 5 minutes?
how: A simpler step: forget 5 minutes. Type 1 minute at 40 words with no mistakes. Then 2 minutes. Add one minute each day.

key: COMP.TYPE.L10.01|How many more words a minute does Level 10 ask than the Typing Certificate? 5, 40, or 15?
how: The skill underneath: Typing Certificate (Computing Level 9). There you held 35 words a minute at 95 for 5 minutes. Level 10 asks for just 5 more words a minute.

key: COMP.TYPE.L10.02|Why learn the Hebrew keyboard? To draw pictures with the letter keys, to type Hebrew words like seforim names, or to type English letters twice as fast?
how: You can type English fast. Now let us add Hebrew, so you can type a dvar Torah sheet, a list of seforim, or a note in Lashon Hakodesh. The good news: your fingers stay in the same place. Each Hebrew letter sits on a key you already know, and you switch the keyboard with two keys.

key: COMP.TYPE.L10.02|Look at the key map. Which English key types ד? D, S, or G?
how: On a Chromebook, hold Ctrl and tap the space bar to switch between English and Hebrew. Each Hebrew letter sits on one English key. Look at the key map: ש sits on A.

how: Watch how Dovid types the word בית (house). He finds ב: it is on C. He finds י: it is on H. He finds ת: it is on the comma key. So he taps C, H, comma. The letters appear from right to left: ב first, on the right.

key: COMP.TYPE.L10.02|When you switch to Hebrew, what changes? The letter each key types, your hand position, or where the keys are?
how: A new way: the Hebrew keyboard is like a second set of name tags on the same seats. The seat (key) stays put; only the tag changes when you switch languages.

key: COMP.TYPE.L10.02|Look at the key map. Which letter is under your left pointer finger, on F? ש, כ, or ג?
how: A simpler step: learn the home row first. Your left hand rests on ש ד ג כ, your right hand on ח ל ך. Say each letter as you press it.

key: COMP.TYPE.L10.02|Which fingers type the Hebrew letters? The same fingers as for those English keys; any finger at all, wherever it lands; or only the two pointer fingers, on every key?
how: The skill underneath: Typing Certificate (Computing Level 9). Your touch typing on the English keys is the base: the Hebrew letters sit on those same keys, so the same fingers reach them.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.01|What does mastering your computer give you? More games to play, a brand-new computer, or your work done faster?
how: A boy who masters his computer gets his work done in half the time. You will open and close tabs, jump between windows, put two windows side by side, change settings, and find any lost file in seconds. These are the moves that make a computer work for you instead of slowing you down.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.01|Which shortcut opens a new tab? Ctrl+W, Alt+Tab, or Ctrl+T?
how: A shortcut is two keys pressed together: hold the first, tap the second. On a Chromebook: Ctrl+T opens a new tab, Ctrl+W closes the tab, and Alt+Tab jumps to your other window.
pic: ⌨️ Ctrl + T

key: COMP.DIG.L10.01|You closed a tab by mistake. Which shortcut brings it back? Ctrl+Shift+T, Ctrl+T, or Ctrl+W?

COMP.DIG.L10.01|Which shortcut closes the tab you are on? Ctrl+T, Alt+Tab, or Ctrl+W?
COMP.DIG.L10.01|The screen is too small to read. Where do you make the text bigger? By closing the lid, by restarting, or in Settings?
COMP.DIG.L10.01|Put the steps to find a lost file in order. The cards say: Open the file from the results., Tap the search key., Type a word from the file name.
COMP.DIG.L10.01|Mordechai writes his book report while checking the book summary. What saves the most time? Closing and reopening each one, printing the summary, or two windows side by side?
COMP.DIG.L10.01|Which shortcut jumps to your other window? Ctrl+T, Ctrl+W, or Alt+Tab?
COMP.DIG.L10.01|What is the fastest way to find a file you saved last week? Scroll through every file, ask a friend, or search for a word in its name?
COMP.DIG.L10.01|Put the steps to use a shortcut in order. The cards say: Let go of both keys., Hold down the first key., Tap the second key.
COMP.DIG.L10.01|In a shortcut like Ctrl+T, what do you do with Ctrl? Hold it down, tap it once, or skip it?
how: A new way: a shortcut is like a secret handshake. Two moves together, in the right order, open the door.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.01|In the simpler step, which one shortcut do you learn first? Ctrl+Shift+T, Alt+[, or Ctrl+T?
how: A simpler step: learn just one shortcut this week, Ctrl+T for a new tab. Use it ten times until it is automatic.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.01|Where are your saved files kept? In storage, in the screen, or in the keyboard?
how: The skill underneath: Inside the Computer (Computing Level 7). The computer keeps your files in storage, and the search key looks through that storage for you.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.02|What is the first step when the computer has a problem? Read the message, ask a helper right away, or tap everything on the screen?
how: Every computer gets stuck sometimes. The boy who knows a calm routine fixes most problems in two minutes, while others wait for help. You will learn the routine: read the message, try the easy fixes one at a time, write down what happened, and only then ask, with the facts ready.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.02|Why change only one thing at a time? So the computer looks busy, so the fixing takes longer, or so you know which fix worked?
how: The easy fixes, in order: close and reopen the app; check the Wi-Fi; restart the computer. Change one thing at a time, so you know which fix worked.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.02|Look at the message. What should you check first? The Wi-Fi, the volume, or the battery?
how: Watch how Chaim fixes a page that will not load. He reads the message: "No internet". He checks the Wi-Fi icon: it is off. He turns Wi-Fi on. The page loads. He writes: "No internet; Wi-Fi was off; turned it on; fixed." Two minutes, no waiting.
pic: ⚠️ No internet connection

key: COMP.DIG.L10.02|An app is frozen and nothing moves. What do you try first? Buy a brand-new computer, close and reopen the app, or hit the keyboard harder?
COMP.DIG.L10.02|You closed and reopened the app and it is still frozen. What is the next easy fix? Close it again, restart the computer, or wait an hour?
COMP.DIG.L10.02|Look at the message. What does it tell you to do? Plug in the charger, turn up the sound, or check the Wi-Fi?
pic: 🔋 Battery 3%: connect to power

key: COMP.DIG.L10.02|Nothing worked. What do you bring when you ask for help? Just "it does not work" and nothing else; nothing, so the helper can start fresh; or what the message said and what you tried?
COMP.DIG.L10.02|Put the fix-it routine in order. The cards say: Ask for help with your notes., Read the message., Try one easy fix at a time and write it down.
COMP.DIG.L10.02|A page will not load. Which easy fix do you try first? Reinstall everything, check the Wi-Fi, or restart?
COMP.DIG.L10.02|Why write down what you tried? To make the note longer and look busy, so a helper does not repeat it, or so he can get a grade for the note?
COMP.DIG.L10.02|You tried three fixes at once and it worked. What is the problem? Nothing; it is fixed for good, it will surely break again, or you do not know which fix worked?
COMP.DIG.L10.02|In the lamp idea, what do you check first? If it is plugged in, the wires inside the wall, or the whole house?
how: A new way: fixing a computer is like finding why a lamp will not light. Is it plugged in? Is the switch on? Is the bulb good? One check at a time, easiest first.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.02|In the simpler step, what are the two words? Read and restart, wait and wish, or run and rest?
how: A simpler step: remember just two words: read, restart. Read the message, and if you do not understand it, restart the computer.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.02|Which skill from Master Your Computer helps you close a stuck app and reopen it? Working with windows, Hebrew letters, or typing fast?
how: The skill underneath: Master Your Computer (Computing Level 10). Knowing settings, windows and search lets you check the Wi-Fi, close a stuck app, and find what went wrong.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.03|Why must an email be clear? It costs more money than a letter, it looks nicer on the screen that way, or the reader cannot ask you what you meant?
how: An email is a letter that arrives in seconds, and the person reads it with no way to ask you what you meant. A clear email gets you a fast answer and shows respect. You will learn the five parts of a good email and when to reply to one person or to everyone. Practice happens in a pretend inbox inside the app.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.03|Which subject line is best for asking about the math test? "Question about Thursday's math test"; "IMPORTANT!!! READ THIS NOW!!!"; or "hi, I have a question for you"?
how: The five parts: a subject line that says what it is about, a polite greeting, one clear request, a thank you, and your name.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.03|Look at Yossi's first email. What is missing at the top? His phone number, a subject line, or a picture?
how: Watch how Yossi fixes his email. It had no subject, said "hey", and gave no thank you. He adds the subject "Missing homework sheet", the greeting "Dear Rabbi Gold,", a clear request "May I have a copy of today's homework sheet?", "Thank you," and his full name.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.03|You need to send your rebbe your essay file. What do you use? A second subject line, a reply all, or an attachment?
COMP.DIG.L10.03|Put the parts of an email in order. The cards say: Thank you and your name., A polite greeting., A subject line that names the topic., One clear request.

COMP.DIG.L10.03|Your yeshiva asks for a reference letter from your rebbe. Which email is best? A long chatty message about his week and no request; a one-word note that just says "letter?" with no subject; or a clear subject, a polite request with the date it is needed, and a thank you?
COMP.DIG.L10.03|What goes in the subject line? A thank you and a goodbye, your full name and your class, or what the email is about?
COMP.DIG.L10.03|When do you use Reply all? Always, so nobody is left out; never, it is always rude; or when everyone needs your answer?
COMP.DIG.L10.03|How should every email to a teacher end? With thank you and your name, with "bye" and a smiley face, or with nothing; just stop typing?
COMP.DIG.L10.03|In the envelope idea, what is like the subject line? The stamp, the letter inside, or the words on the outside?
how: A new way: an email is like a letter in an envelope. The subject is what you write on the outside of the envelope; the greeting, request and thank you are the letter inside.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.03|What are the two simple rules? A picture and a link, a subject and a thank you, or capitals and emojis?
how: A simpler step: just remember two rules. Every email has a subject. Every email says thank you.

key: COMP.DIG.L10.03|What does an email borrow from a formal letter? A greeting and a closing, a page border, or a table of numbers?
how: The skill underneath: Professional Documents (Computing Level 8). There you laid out a formal letter. An email to a rebbe or a school uses the same respectful parts.

key: COMP.TYPE.L11.01|What is the hard part of copying from paper? Finding the keys, keeping your place, or turning the computer on?
how: Much of real work is copying from paper: a rebbe's handwritten sheet, a page of notes, a form. The hard part is not speed; it is keeping your place. In this lesson you learn how to set up the paper, keep your place with a card, and still reach 40 words a minute with 96 of every 100 words right.

key: COMP.TYPE.L11.01|Where does the paper go? Under the keyboard, flat on your lap, or on a stand at eye level?
how: Set the paper on a stand next to the screen, at eye level, so your head does not bob up and down. Slide a card or ruler under the line you are typing, and move it down one line at a time.

key: COMP.TYPE.L11.01|Look at Avi's test. What is his accuracy, out of 100? 97, 96, or 94?
how: Watch how Avi checks his copy test. He typed 1,050 letters and spaces in 5 minutes: 1,050 ÷ 5 = 210 words; 210 ÷ 5 = 42 words a minute. 6 of the 210 words had a mistake: 204 ÷ 210 = 97 out of 100. Speed 42, accuracy 97: he passes.

key: COMP.TYPE.L11.01|Moshe keeps skipping a line when he copies. What helps most? A bigger, brighter screen; typing much faster; or a card under the line?

COMP.TYPE.L11.01|Your rebbe hands you his handwritten list of 30 seforim for the shul library. A word is hard to read. What do you do? Ask him what it says, guess a word, or skip it?
COMP.TYPE.L11.01|What tool keeps your place on the paper? A second screen, a louder keyboard, or a card under the line?
COMP.TYPE.L11.01|A copy test: 1,000 letters and spaces in 5 minutes, 8 of 200 words with a mistake. Accuracy out of 100? 96, 98, or 92?
COMP.TYPE.L11.01|Why put the paper at eye level? So it looks neat on the desk, so the teacher can see it, or so your head does not bob up and down?
COMP.TYPE.L11.01|In the reading-aloud idea, what does your finger do? Turns the page for you, taps on the table, or keeps your place?
how: A new way: copying is like reading aloud to a friend while he writes. You keep a finger on the line so you never lose your spot. The card does the same job for your eyes.

key: COMP.TYPE.L11.01|In the simpler step, how many lines do you copy first? Three, thirty, or one hundred?
how: A simpler step: copy just three lines, slowly, with the card. Count your mistakes. When you have none, copy five lines.

key: COMP.TYPE.L11.01|What speed did Speed Builder ask for? 40 words a minute, 20 words a minute, or 80 words a minute?
how: The skill underneath: Speed Builder (Computing Level 10). There you held 40 words a minute for 5 minutes. Copying uses the same speed; only the eyes look at paper instead of a screen.

key: COMP.TYPE.L11.02|On the ten-key, which numbers are in the top row? 1, 2 and 3; 7, 8 and 9; or 4, 5 and 6?
how: A new way: the number pad is like a phone keypad turned upside down. On a phone 1, 2, 3 are on top; on the ten-key 7, 8, 9 are on top. Once you know that, your fingers settle in fast.

key: COMP.TYPE.L11.02|Where did you type numbers in Numbers and Symbols? The ten-key pad on the right, the number row above the letters, or the touch screen?
how: The skill underneath: Numbers and Symbols (Computing Level 8). There you typed the number row by touch. The ten-key is a second, faster home for the same numbers.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.01|What do speed tools save you? Money in the bank, hours of work, or battery power?
how: The fastest workers do not work harder; they use the tools built into the computer. With a few shortcuts you can find any word in a long document, change a mistake everywhere at once, undo anything, and copy whole paragraphs. These tools save you hours every week.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.01|Look at the notes. If you search for "shul", how many matches are there? 1, 3, or 2?
how: Ctrl+F opens a find box. Type a word and the document jumps to it and counts how many times it appears. Ctrl+H finds a word and replaces it with another, one at a time or everywhere at once.
pic: Notes: The shul trip leaves at 9. Bring water to the shul. The shul bus waits by the gate.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.01|Look at the list. If you replace "kugel" with "cake" everywhere, how many words change? 4, 5, or 3?
how: Watch how Mendy uses Replace all on his Shabbos menu. He wants every "salad" to say "coleslaw". He presses Ctrl+H, types "salad" in the find box and "coleslaw" in the replace box, and taps Replace all. One tap, and every match is fixed.
pic: List: kugel, kugel pan, potato kugel, salad, kugel spoon

key: COMP.DIG.L11.01|Which shortcut undoes your last change? Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Z, or Ctrl+Y?
COMP.DIG.L11.01|You undid too much. Which shortcut redoes it? Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Y, or Ctrl+Z?
COMP.DIG.L11.01|You spelled your friend's name wrong 12 times in a long story. What is fastest? Retyping the whole story, find and replace, or fixing each one by hand?
COMP.DIG.L11.01|Which shortcut opens the find box? Ctrl+F, Ctrl+Z, or Ctrl+H?
COMP.DIG.L11.01|Put the steps to replace a word everywhere in order. The cards say: Tap Replace all., Press Ctrl+H., Type the old word and the new word.
COMP.DIG.L11.01|You are typing your class's Chanukah program and need the same welcome line on five pages. What is fastest? Copy it once and paste it, type it five times, or print it five times?
COMP.DIG.L11.01|Which shortcut finds and replaces? Ctrl+Y, Ctrl+H, or Ctrl+F?
COMP.DIG.L11.01|Look at the notes. If you replace "shul" with "school" everywhere, how many words change? 3, 4, or 1?
pic: Notes: The shul trip leaves at 9. Bring water to the shul. The shul bus waits by the gate.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.01|Which pair copies and pastes? Ctrl+C then Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Z then Ctrl+Y, or Ctrl+F then Ctrl+H?
COMP.DIG.L11.01|In the red-pen idea, how many sweeps fix every page? One per page, one, or none?
how: A new way: find and replace is like a teacher with a red pen who fixes the same mistake on every page in one sweep, instead of page by page.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.01|What does Ctrl+Z do? Closes the window, takes back the last step, or saves the whole file?
how: A simpler step: learn just Ctrl+Z. Any time something goes wrong, Ctrl+Z takes back the last step. Try it ten times.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.01|How do you press Ctrl+F? Tap F, then tap Ctrl; hold Ctrl and tap F; or press them one minute apart?
how: The skill underneath: Master Your Computer (Computing Level 10). There you learned that a shortcut is: hold the first key, tap the second. Every speed tool here works the same way.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.02|What does a clear file system give you? More free storage, a faster internet, or any file in seconds?
how: By tenth grade you have hundreds of files, and you share some of them with rebbeim, teachers and chavrusas. A clear system means you find any file in seconds and never lose work. You will learn folders, smart file names, the three ways to share, and how to get back an older copy. Practice happens in a pretend drive in the app.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.02|Look at the files. Which one is oldest? Essay final, Essay draft, or Notes chapter 1?
how: Start a file name with the date, year first: 2026-11-02 Essay final. Files then line up in time order by themselves, oldest first.

how: Watch how Shlomo shares his essay. His rebbe should only read it: Shlomo shares "view". His chavrusa should suggest changes: "comment". His partner on a group project writes with him: "edit". He gives each person the least they need.

COMP.DIG.L11.02|You and Dovid write a Purim shpiel together on one shared file. Which share does Dovid need? Edit, view, or comment?
COMP.DIG.L11.02|Why start a file name with the date, year first? It looks fancy, files sort in time order, or it is a rule by law?
COMP.DIG.L11.02|What should you give each person you share with? Edit to everyone, the least they need, or nothing at all?
COMP.DIG.L11.02|Look at the files. Which one was made in September? Essay draft, Notes chapter 1, or Essay final?
pic:

key: COMP.DIG.L11.02|In the simpler step, what does every file name start with? Today's date, your own name, or the word "file"?
how: A simpler step: just name every new file with today's date first, year-month-day. Do only that this week.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.02|How did Master Your Computer find a lost file? By restarting it, with the search key, or by asking a friend?
how: The skill underneath: Master Your Computer (Computing Level 10). There you found files with search. A clear folder system means you find them even without search.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.03|How do most break-ins happen? By guessing the color, by breaking the screen, or by tricking someone?
how: Your accounts hold your schoolwork, your messages and, one day, your money. People try to break into accounts every day, mostly by tricking someone. You will learn the four locks that stop almost all of it: two-step sign-in, updates, a password manager, and spotting a fake message.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.03|With two-step sign-in, what does a thief need besides your password? Your shoe size, nothing more at all, or a code sent to you?
how: Two-step sign-in means a thief needs two things: your password and a code sent to your phone or a key. Even if he steals the password, he is stuck without the code.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.03|Look at the message. Which clue in the sender address shows it is fake? The ".com" at the end, the number 1 in "schoo1", or the word "help" in it?
how: Watch how Gavriel checks a message. The sender is "tashbar-schoo1.com", with the number 1 instead of the letter l. It says "TODAY!" to rush him. It asks for his password. Three warning signs: he does not click, and he tells his teacher.
pic: From: help@tashbar-schoo1.com\nSubject: Your account will close TODAY!\nClick here and type your password to keep it.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.03|Look at the message. How many warning signs does it have? 3, 1, or 0?
pic: From: help@tashbar-schoo1.com\nSubject: Your account will close TODAY!\nClick here and type your password to keep it.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.03|Your computer says an update is ready. What do you do? Install it soon, ignore it for a year, or turn it off forever?
COMP.DIG.L11.03|What does a password manager do? Makes every password exactly the same; keeps a strong, different password for each account; or shares your passwords with your friends?
COMP.DIG.L11.03|A message asks you to type your password to "win a prize". What do you do? Type it in quickly; do not click, and tell a teacher; or send it to a friend first?
COMP.DIG.L11.03|Put the steps for a strange message in order. The cards say: Tell a teacher or Abba., Stop: do not click anything., Check the sender, the rush and what it asks for.

COMP.DIG.L11.03|Zeidy gets a text saying his bank account is locked and he must click a link now. What do you tell him? Call the bank on its real number, reply with his PIN number, or click the link right away?
COMP.DIG.L11.03|What does two-step sign-in add? A second check after the password, a much longer password, or a brand-new email address?
COMP.DIG.L11.03|Which is a warning sign of a fake message? It has your correct name, it rushes you, or it arrives in the morning?
COMP.DIG.L11.03|Why install updates soon? They close holes thieves use, they make it run slower, or they change the colors?
COMP.DIG.L11.03|In the house idea, what is a fake message like? A second lock on the door, a stranger asking for your key, or a new window in the wall?
how: A new way: your account is like your house. A password is the lock on the door. Two-step sign-in is a second lock. Updates fix broken windows. A fake message is a stranger asking for your key.

key: COMP.DIG.L11.03|What is the one rule? Always click every link you get, share your passwords with friends, or never type a password after clicking a message link?
how: A simpler step: one rule for this week: never type a password after clicking a link in a message.

key: COMP.TYPE.L12.01|What does Typing Certificate II need? 65 words a minute at 97, 40 words a minute at 95, or 50 words a minute at 96?
how: This is your second typing certificate, and it is a serious one: 50 words a minute with 96 of every 100 words right, held for 5 minutes. That is faster than most adults type. With it, notes, essays and forms stop being a chore, and the certificate is something you can show a yeshiva or an employer.

key: COMP.TYPE.L12.01|Look at the test. How many words a minute? 52, 260, or 50?
how: The math is the same as before. 1,300 letters and spaces ÷ 5 = 260 words. 260 words ÷ 5 minutes = 52 words a minute.
pic: Certificate test: 5 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 1300\nWords with a mistake: 8 of 260

key: COMP.TYPE.L12.01|Look at the test again. Does it earn Typing Certificate II? Yes, both pass; no, accuracy is too low; or no, speed is too low?
how: Watch how a typist decides pass or fail. Speed: 52. Accuracy: 8 of 260 words wrong, so 252 ÷ 260 = 0.969, about 97 out of 100. Speed 52 is at least 50, and 97 is at least 96. Both pass, so he earns the certificate.
pic: Certificate test: 5 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 1300\nWords with a mistake: 8 of 260

key: COMP.TYPE.L12.01|Look at this test. How many words a minute? 25, 50, or 250?
pic: Certificate test: 5 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 1250\nWords with a mistake: 5 of 250

pic: Certificate test: 5 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 1250\nWords with a mistake: 5 of 250

key: COMP.TYPE.L12.01|Which result earns the certificate? 48 at 99, 55 at 94, or 51 at 97?

COMP.TYPE.L12.01|Your speed is 50 but your accuracy is stuck at 94. What should you practice? Hard words slowly until they are right; nothing; 94 is close enough; or only speed drills, faster and faster?

COMP.TYPE.L12.01|Put the steps for a certificate test in order. The cards say: Read your results and print the certificate if you passed., Warm up for 2 minutes., Type the 5-minute passage without stopping.

COMP.TYPE.L12.01|Binyomin wants a summer office job at his uncle's business. What can he show to prove he types well? His typing certificate with speed and accuracy, a photo of his keyboard at home, or a list of the games he plays?
COMP.TYPE.L12.01|A typist types 1,400 letters and spaces in 5 minutes. Words a minute? 56, 70, or 280?
COMP.TYPE.L12.01|He typed 300 words with 12 mistakes. Accuracy out of 100? 88, 96, or 99?
COMP.TYPE.L12.01|For how long must you hold the speed? 30 seconds, 5 minutes, or 1 minute?
COMP.TYPE.L12.01|In the bicycle idea, what happens if accuracy is low? You do not pass, you pass anyway, or you get a bonus?
how: A new way: speed and accuracy are like the two wheels of a bicycle. If either one is flat, you do not get anywhere. The certificate needs both wheels full.

key: COMP.TYPE.L12.01|In the simpler step, how long is the first run at 50? 10 minutes, 1 minute, or 5 minutes?
how: A simpler step: hold 50 words a minute for just 1 minute, with 96 right. Then 2 minutes, then 3. Add a minute each week.

key: COMP.TYPE.L12.01|How many more words a minute does Certificate II need than Copy from Paper? 50, 5, or 10?
how: The skill underneath: Copy from Paper (Computing Level 11). There you held 40 words a minute at 96 while copying. The certificate keeps that accuracy and adds 10 words a minute.

key: COMP.DIG.L12.01|Why use headings in a long paper? So the paper is many pages longer, so readers find any part fast, or so the paper looks more colorful?
how: A research paper is too long to scroll through. Real writers use headings, a table of contents, page numbers and footnotes, so readers find any part fast and see where facts came from. And when your rebbe or a friend checks it, comments and suggested edits let them help without erasing your words.

key: COMP.DIG.L12.01|Look at the outline. On which page does the chapter "How Bees Talk" start? 3, 4, or 7?
how: Mark each chapter title as Heading 1 and smaller section titles as Heading 2. The table of contents is then built from your headings, with page numbers, in one click.

key: COMP.DIG.L12.01|Where do you say where a fact came from, without breaking your sentence? A new chapter, the title page, or a footnote?
COMP.DIG.L12.01|Your rebbe wants to suggest changes without erasing your words. What does he use? Suggested edits and comments, delete and type over, or a brand-new file?
COMP.DIG.L12.01|Put the steps for a table of contents in order. The cards say: Insert the table of contents., Mark each chapter title as Heading 1., Update the table after you add pages.
COMP.DIG.L12.01|Your 15-page history paper on the Jews of early America needs page numbers. Where do you add them? In the title of the paper, typed on each page by hand, or in the header or footer?
COMP.DIG.L12.01|Which style marks a chapter title? Normal text, Heading 2, or Heading 1?
COMP.DIG.L12.01|Look at the outline. On which page does "Conclusion" start? 7, 1, or 4?

key: COMP.DIG.L12.01|What is the table of contents built from? The page numbers, the headings, or the footnotes?
COMP.DIG.L12.01|In the shul idea, what is like the table of contents? The parking lot, a single door, or the map in the lobby?
how: A new way: headings are like the signs in a big shul building: "Main Shul", "Beis Medrash", "Library". The table of contents is the map in the lobby that lists every sign and its floor.

key: COMP.DIG.L12.01|In the simpler step, what do you mark? All of the footnotes, every word in bold, or chapter titles as Heading 1?
how: A simpler step: today only mark your chapter titles as Heading 1. Nothing else.

key: COMP.DIG.L12.01|What did Professional Documents teach that long papers use again? Passwords, headings, or typing speed?
how: The skill underneath: Professional Documents (Computing Level 8). There you used headings and tables in a letter. A long paper uses the same headings, many more times.

key: COMP.DIG.L12.02|What do search tools do for you? Show you many more ads, cut results down to what you need, or make the computer run much faster?
how: A plain search gives you thousands of results, most of them useless. A few search tools cut that down to exactly what you need: an exact phrase, leaving a word out, and searching one website you trust. You will practice on a pretend search page inside the app, so nothing here goes online.

key: COMP.DIG.L12.02|Look at the search. Which result is kept? Lightning (movie) cast list, How Lightning Forms, or Lightning Movie Reviews?
how: A minus sign right before a word leaves out every result with that word. Searching lightning -movie shows pages about lightning, but none about the movie.
pic:
Search: lightning -movie
Result 1: Lightning Movie Reviews
Result 2: How Lightning Forms — Science Museum
Result 3: Lightning (movie) cast list

key: COMP.DIG.L12.02|Look at the search. Which result matches both rules? Bees for sale, honey and bees recipe blog, or Honey Bees in Winter?
how: Watch how Tzvi searches for a trusted bee page. He types "honey bees" in quotation marks, so the words must appear together, and adds site:museum.org, so only that website counts. One result matches both rules.
pic:
Search: "honey bees" site:museum.org
Result 1: honey and bees recipe blog — cooking.com
Result 2: Honey Bees in Winter — museum.org
Result 3: Bees for sale — shop.com

key: COMP.DIG.L12.02|Look at the bee search. Why is the recipe blog left out? It is not on museum.org, it has no title at all, or it is too old to show?
pic:
Search: "honey bees" site:museum.org
Result 1: honey and bees recipe blog — cooking.com
Result 2: Honey Bees in Winter — museum.org
Result 3: Bees for sale — shop.com

key: COMP.DIG.L12.02|You want the exact words "Rambam's medicine" together. What do you add? Site: in front, quotation marks around them, or a minus sign before them?
COMP.DIG.L12.02|Look at the lightning search. How many results does the minus sign remove? 1, 3, or 2?
pic:
Search: lightning -movie
Result 1: Lightning Movie Reviews
Result 2: How Lightning Forms — Science Museum
Result 3: Lightning (movie) cast list

key: COMP.DIG.L12.02|You found the right paragraph on a long page but lost it. Which shortcut finds a word on the page? Ctrl+T, Ctrl+F, or Ctrl+W?
COMP.DIG.L12.02|Put the steps of a smart search in order. The cards say: Check the source before you trust it., Type the main words., Add a tool: quotes, minus or site:.
COMP.DIG.L12.02|For a Shabbos table talk on the Wright brothers you keep getting a toy store. What do you add? "toy store", -toy, or site:toys.com?
COMP.DIG.L12.02|What does a minus sign before a word do? Searches inside just one website, leaves out results with that word, or finds only pages with that one word?
COMP.DIG.L12.02|Which search looks only at museum.org? Museum bees, site:museum.org bees, or -museum bees?
COMP.DIG.L12.02|After you find a page, what do you still do? Check the source, trust it right away, or share it with everyone?
COMP.DIG.L12.02|In the librarian idea, what is like the minus sign? "books about bees", "from the museum shelf", or "not the cookbooks"?
how: A new way: a search is like asking a librarian. "Books about bees" gets a cart full. "The book called Honey Bees in Winter, from the museum shelf, not the cookbooks" gets one.

key: COMP.DIG.L12.02|In the simpler step, which tool do you learn? Site:, quotation marks, or the minus sign?
how: A simpler step: learn only quotation marks this week. Put them around any phrase that must stay together.

key: COMP.DIG.L12.02|Which question comes from Judge a Source? Who wrote it, what color is the page, or how many results?
how: The skill underneath: Judge a Source (Computing Level 6). Search tools find pages fast, but you still ask: who wrote it, does it match good sources, is it selling something?

key: COMP.DIG.L12.03|Who do these tools help? Only boys who are computer experts, nobody; they are just for show, or anyone who finds reading or typing hard?
how: Computers have tools that help anyone who finds reading or typing hard: a grandfather with weak eyes, a friend with a broken arm, or you on a tired day. You will learn to make text bigger, have the computer read aloud, type by speaking, and make your own documents easy for everyone to read.

key: COMP.DIG.L12.03|Your arm is in a cast and you need to write your essay. Which tool helps? Dictation, Select-to-speak, or Ctrl and minus?
COMP.DIG.L12.03|Why add a short description to a picture in your document? So a screen reader can tell what it shows, so it prints in bright color, or so the picture fills the page?
COMP.DIG.L12.03|Which keys make a page smaller again? Ctrl and W, Ctrl and minus, or Ctrl and plus?
COMP.DIG.L12.03|White text on a pale yellow background is hard to read. What should you change? Add even more yellow, use dark text on a light background, or make the text smaller?
COMP.DIG.L12.03|Put the steps to have a paragraph read aloud in order. The cards say: Hold Search and tap S., Turn on Select-to-speak in Settings., Choose the paragraph to hear.

COMP.DIG.L12.03|Your class makes a Purim newsletter for the whole school. What makes it easy for everyone to read? Clear headings and picture descriptions, long paragraphs in all capitals, or tiny fancy letters everywhere?
COMP.DIG.L12.03|Which tool reads text aloud? Dictation, Select-to-speak, or Ctrl and plus?
COMP.DIG.L12.03|Which tool types what you say? High contrast, Select-to-speak, or Dictation?
COMP.DIG.L12.03|What helps a screen reader understand your document? Bright colors everywhere, headings and picture descriptions, or bigger margins?
COMP.DIG.L12.03|In the simpler step, what do you learn first? Headings, Search and D, or Ctrl and plus?
how: A simpler step: learn just Ctrl and plus today. Make a page bigger, then Ctrl and minus to go back.

key: COMP.DIG.L12.03|What do headings do for a screen reader? Let it jump from part to part, speed up your typing, or change the page colors?
how: The skill underneath: Long Documents (Computing Level 12). Headings you add for a table of contents also let a screen reader jump from part to part.

key: COMP.TYPE.L13.01|What is the real skill of notes while listening? Catching the main ideas, recording the speaker, or typing every single word?
how: In twelfth grade and in college you will sit through long shiurim, lectures and meetings. Good notes let you remember and review them later. A speaker talks much faster than anyone can type, so the skill is not typing every word; it is catching the main ideas, fast and clear, with headings and short forms.

key: COMP.TYPE.L13.01|Look at the short forms. What does b/c mean? Before, between, or because?
how: Short forms save time: w/ means with, b/c means because, an arrow means "leads to", ex means example. Use the same short forms every time so you can read them later.
pic: Short forms\nw/ = with · b/c = because · → = leads to · ex = example · # = number

key: COMP.TYPE.L13.01|Look at the rates. About how many words of every 10 the speaker says can you type? About 4, all 10, or about 9?
how: Watch how Yehuda takes notes. The speaker says: "Rain falls because water vapor cools and turns back into drops; for example, the drops on a cold cup." Yehuda types: "Rain b/c vapor cools → drops. ex: cold cup." Eleven words became seven, and every idea is still there.
pic: A speaker talks about 130 words a minute.\nYou type about 50 words a minute.

key: COMP.TYPE.L13.01|Look at the short forms. Which note means "rain leads to floods"? Rain w/ floods, rain → floods, or rain # floods?
pic: Short forms\nw/ = with · b/c = because · → = leads to · ex = example · # = number

key: COMP.TYPE.L13.01|The rebbe says, "Let me tell you a funny story about my trip," then gives the main lesson. What do you type? The main lesson, the whole story word for word, or nothing at all?
COMP.TYPE.L13.01|When is the best time to fix and fill in your notes? Never; the notes are done, right after the talk, or a month after the talk ends?
COMP.TYPE.L13.01|How do you show a new topic in your notes? A heading on its own line; one long run-on sentence; or a fresh, empty blank page?
COMP.TYPE.L13.01|Put the note-taking steps in order. The cards say: Type the main ideas under each heading., Type a heading for the topic., Fix and fill in the notes right after.
COMP.TYPE.L13.01|At the yeshiva open house the menahel explains the daily schedule. What are the best notes? Just the word "schedule"; times and places, w/ short forms; or every word he says?
COMP.TYPE.L13.01|Look at the short forms. What does w/ mean? With, without, or which?
pic: Short forms\nw/ = with · b/c = because · → = leads to · ex = example · # = number

key: COMP.TYPE.L13.01|Why can you not type every word of a talk? Speakers talk faster than you type, typing is not allowed in a talk, or the keyboard is too small?

COMP.TYPE.L13.01|Which note is best for "We need to bring the forms because the office closes Friday"? We need to bring the forms because the office closes Friday, bring forms b/c office closes Fri, or forms?
COMP.TYPE.L13.01|In the packing idea, how do you write each item? In a full story, in a few words, or not at all?
how: A new way: notes are like a packing list for a trip. You do not write "I will take the blue shirt that Zeidy bought me for Pesach"; you write "blue shirt". Only what you need, in few words.

key: COMP.TYPE.L13.01|In the simpler step, what do you type first? Only the headings, the short forms list, or every single word?
how: A simpler step: practice with a 2-minute recording. Type only the headings first. Next time, add one main idea under each.

key: COMP.TYPE.L13.01|Why does fast touch typing help with notes? It records the talk for you, your eyes and ears stay on the speaker, or it makes the talk itself shorter?
how: The skill underneath: Typing Certificate II (Computing Level 12). Typing 50 words a minute without looking lets your eyes and ears stay on the speaker while your fingers write.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.01|Why learn to set up a computer? To change the computer's color, soon nobody will do it for you, or it is a fun game to play?
how: Soon you will get a new computer for yeshiva, college or work, and nobody will set it up for you. A computer set up well is safe, fast and ready for learning. You will learn the order: power and Wi-Fi, sign in, updates, only the programs you need, and the settings your school wants.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.01|When do you run updates on a new computer? Right after signing in, after using it a month, or never; it is new?
how: Updates come right after you sign in, before you install anything. A brand-new computer may have waited months in a box, and updates close the safety holes found since then.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.01|What does Naftali install? Only approved programs, every free program he finds, or nothing at all?
how: Watch how Naftali sets up his new laptop. He charges it, connects to the Wi-Fi, signs in, and runs every update. Then he installs only the three programs his yeshiva approved, turns on the school's filter and safety settings, and removes the games that came with it.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.01|The new laptop came with five games you do not need. What do you do? Remove them, keep them all, or hide them in a folder?
COMP.DIG.L13.01|Where do you get a program you need? From a pop-up ad, from a stranger's link, or from the official store or the school?
COMP.DIG.L13.01|The yeshiva asks every boy to turn on its filter and safety settings. When do you do it? During setup, after a year, or only if asked twice?
COMP.DIG.L13.01|Put the setup steps in order. The cards say: Install only approved programs and set the school settings., Charge and connect to Wi-Fi., Sign in and run every update.
COMP.DIG.L13.01|Why run updates before installing programs? To change the screen language, to fill up the empty disk, or to close safety holes first?
COMP.DIG.L13.01|Which programs go on a school computer? Whatever a friend sends, only approved ones, or any that look fun?
COMP.DIG.L13.01|In the dorm idea, what is like running updates? Locking the door, bringing in a couch, or painting the walls?
how: A new way: setting up a computer is like moving into a new dorm room. First the lights and heat, then you lock the door, then you bring in only what you need.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.01|What are the three words in order? Update, games, power; programs, power, update; or power, update, programs?
how: A simpler step: remember three words in order: power, update, programs.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.01|Which Fix It Yourself habit helps during setup? Skip the updates, read every message, or tap everything fast?
how: The skill underneath: Fix It Yourself (Computing Level 10). Setup uses the same calm habits: read every message, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.02|Look at Yaakov's copies. How many copies does he have? 1, 3, or 2?
how: Three copies means the original plus two backups. Two kinds of storage means not all on one device: for example the laptop and an online drive. One somewhere else means one copy is not in the same building, so a fire or a theft cannot take them all.
pic:
Yaakov's essay is saved in:
1. the laptop
2. the school drive (online)
3. a USB stick kept at home

key: COMP.DIG.L13.02|Look at Ephraim's copies. Does he pass 3-2-1? Yes, it is in two folders; no, everything is on one laptop; or yes, two copies are enough?
how: Watch how we check Yaakov. Copies: laptop, school drive, USB stick, so 3. Kinds of storage: the laptop, an online drive and a USB stick, so more than 2. Somewhere else: the online drive and the stick at home are both away from his school bag. Yaakov passes 3-2-1.
pic: Ephraim's essay is saved in:\n1. the laptop\n2. a second folder on the same laptop

key: COMP.DIG.L13.02|Look at Ephraim's copies. How many kinds of storage does he use? 3, 2, or 1?
pic: Ephraim's essay is saved in:\n1. the laptop\n2. a second folder on the same laptop

key: COMP.DIG.L13.02|Your laptop is stolen. Which backup still has your work? The school drive online, a second folder on that laptop, or the trash folder?
COMP.DIG.L13.02|You deleted the newest page of your shared essay by mistake. What brings it back fastest? A USB stick from last month, version history, or retyping the whole page?
COMP.DIG.L13.02|Put the steps to restore a lost file in order. The cards say: Open it to check it is the right version., Find the file in your backup., Copy it back to your laptop.
COMP.DIG.L13.02|The shul office keeps its member list on one old computer. What do you suggest? Print it out one time, add an online copy and a stick kept at home, or keep it just the way it is?
COMP.DIG.L13.02|Look at Yaakov's copies. Which one is online? The school drive, the laptop, or the USB stick?
pic:
Yaakov's essay is saved in:
1. the laptop
2. the school drive (online)
3. a USB stick kept at home

key: COMP.DIG.L13.02|Why are two folders on one laptop not a real backup? Folders cannot hold essays, folders are too small, or one broken laptop loses both?
COMP.DIG.L13.02|In the key idea, what is like the copy kept somewhere else? The key with Zeidy, the lock on the door, or the key on your keyring?
how: A new way: backups are like a spare house key. One on your keyring, one in a drawer at home, one with Zeidy across town. Lose your keyring and you still get in.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.02|In the simpler step, where does the first backup go? The same folder, the school drive, or the trash?
how: A simpler step: today, put one copy of your most important file on the school drive. That is your first backup.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.02|Which Shared Files tool brings back older copies? Version history, the share button, or Ctrl+T?
how: The skill underneath: Shared Files (Computing Level 11). Your folders and version history on the school drive already give you one backup and older copies.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.03|Who might look you up soon? Only your closest friends; nobody ever looks you up; or a yeshiva, a college or a boss?
how: Soon a yeshiva, a college or a boss may look you up. What they find should show who you really are: a boy with good middos who uses technology carefully. You will learn what others can see, how to keep your details private, and why the school and your parents set limits on online use.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.03|Which detail should you never share with strangers online? Your home address, the weather today, or your favorite sefer?
how: Privacy settings decide who can see your details. Keep them tight: share your name only where it is needed, and never share your address, phone number or schedule with strangers.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.03|Meir's friend does not want the photo shared. What does Meir do? Post it anyway, not post it, or post it later?
how: Watch how Meir decides before he posts a photo from the yeshiva trip. He asks: Would my rebbe be proud of it? Did everyone in it agree? Could it embarrass someone later? One "no" means he does not post it.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.03|You deleted an old post. Is it gone forever? Yes, it is gone after a day; maybe not: someone may have copied it; or yes, it is always gone?
COMP.DIG.L13.03|A website asks for your phone number to see a funny video. What do you do? Leave the site, type it in, or type a friend's number?

COMP.DIG.L13.03|Why do the school and your parents limit which sites and apps you use? To make you bored on purpose all day; for no reason that anyone knows; or to protect your time, your learning and your middos?
COMP.DIG.L13.03|Which privacy setting is safest for anything you post? Only people you choose, everyone in the world, or whoever happens to find it?
COMP.DIG.L13.03|Put Meir's three questions in order. The cards say: Could it embarrass someone later?, Would my rebbe be proud of it?, Did everyone in it agree?
COMP.DIG.L13.03|A college asks for your email in an application. Which address is best? A random string of numbers, your first and last name, or "coolguy4ever"?
COMP.DIG.L13.03|What is Meir's first question before posting? Would my rebbe be proud of it, how many likes will it get, or is it funny?
COMP.DIG.L13.03|Who decides which sites and apps you use? The school and your parents, any website you visit, or your friends?
COMP.DIG.L13.03|Which detail is safe to keep private? None of them; all are fine; only the home address; or all of these: address, phone, schedule?
COMP.DIG.L13.03|In the shul idea, can you take back words once said? No; yes, if you whisper; or yes, easily?
how: A new way: what you put online is like words said in a shul full of people. You cannot take them back, and many may remember them.

key: COMP.DIG.L13.03|What is the one rule? Share everything you like, never share anything ever, or ask "would my rebbe be proud of it?"?
how: A simpler step: one rule: before you share anything, ask "Would my rebbe be proud of it?"

key: COMP.DIG.L13.03|What did Digital Footprint teach? What is shared can stay a long time, how to type faster on the keys, or how to make graphs in a sheet?
how: The skill underneath: Digital Footprint (Computing Level 7). There you learned that what gets saved and shared can stay for a long time. My Name Online uses that to guard who you are.

key: COMP.TYPE.L14.01|What is the Level 14 goal? 50 words a minute at 96, 60 words a minute at 97, or 80 words a minute at 90?
how: Professional typists, office workers and court reporters type 60 words a minute or more, with almost no mistakes. Reaching 60 at 97 out of 100 for 5 minutes puts you with them. In college it means notes, papers and emails take a fraction of the time, and in a job interview it is a skill you can prove.

key: COMP.TYPE.L14.01|Look at the test. How many words a minute? 62, 60, or 310?
how: The math does not change: 1,550 letters and spaces ÷ 5 = 310 words. 310 ÷ 5 minutes = 62 words a minute.
pic: Professional test: 5 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 1550\nWords with a mistake: 9 of 310

key: COMP.TYPE.L14.01|Look at the test. Does it pass Level 14? Yes, both reach the goal; no, accuracy is too low; or no, speed is too low?
how: Watch how we judge this test. Speed 62. Mistakes: 9 of 310 words, so 301 ÷ 310 = 0.971, about 97 out of 100. 62 is at least 60 and 97 is at least 97: it passes, right at the accuracy line.
pic: Professional test: 5 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 1550\nWords with a mistake: 9 of 310

key: COMP.TYPE.L14.01|Look at this test. How many words a minute? 62, 58, or 290?
pic: Professional test: 5 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 1450\nWords with a mistake: 3 of 290

key: COMP.TYPE.L14.01|Look at the same test. Does it pass Level 14? Yes, it passes; no, accuracy is too low; or no, speed is too low?
pic: Professional test: 5 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 1450\nWords with a mistake: 3 of 290

key: COMP.TYPE.L14.01|Which result passes Level 14? 58 at 99, 66 at 95, or 61 at 98?
COMP.TYPE.L14.01|At 60 words a minute, your mistakes come from rushing hard words. What helps? Ignore the mistakes completely, type everything even faster, or type hard words slowly in drills?

COMP.TYPE.L14.01|Put a week of speed training in order. The cards say: Take a full 5-minute test on Friday., Warm up and drill your slow words each day., Note your speed and mistakes after each drill.

COMP.TYPE.L14.01|A job ad for an office assistant asks for "50+ words per minute". You type 62 at 97. What do you write on the application? Nothing about typing at all; typing: 62 words per minute, 97% accuracy; or "I type pretty fast, I think"?
COMP.TYPE.L14.01|1,600 letters and spaces in 5 minutes. Words a minute? 64, 80, or 320?
COMP.TYPE.L14.01|He typed 300 words with 6 mistakes. Accuracy out of 100? 94, 96, or 98?
COMP.TYPE.L14.01|How many more words a minute is Level 14 than Certificate II? 10, 5, or 20?
COMP.TYPE.L14.01|In the runner idea, what is like your "hill"? The keyboard itself, the whole passage every time, or the few words that slow you?
how: A new way: going from 50 to 60 is like a runner cutting seconds off his time. He does not run harder everywhere; he finds the one hill that slows him and trains on it.

key: COMP.TYPE.L14.01|In the simpler step, how long do you hold 60 first? 1 minute, 10 minutes, or 5 minutes?
how: A simpler step: hold 60 for just 1 minute with no more than 1 mistake. When that is easy, go to 2 minutes.

key: COMP.TYPE.L14.01|What did Certificate II ask for? 50 at 96, 60 at 97, or 35 at 95?
how: The skill underneath: Typing Certificate II (Computing Level 12). There you held 50 at 96 for 5 minutes. The same habits, plus drills on slow words, carry you to 60.

key: COMP.DIG.L14.01|Where do you hand in college work? By phone to the office, on the course website, or by mail in an envelope?
how: College runs on a course website: the syllabus, the readings, the deadlines and the place you hand in work. Many courses are online, from colleges in other time zones. A student who knows the toolkit never misses a deadline by accident. You will learn file types, time zones and calendar reminders.

key: COMP.DIG.L14.01|Look at the time zones. How many hours behind New York is Denver? 3, 2, or 1?
how: When a course is in another time zone, turn its deadline into your own time. Baltimore is on Eastern time. Places west of you are behind: Chicago is 1 hour behind, Los Angeles 3 hours behind. So 5:00 PM in Chicago is 6:00 PM in Baltimore.
pic:
Time zones (hours behind New York)
New York (Eastern): 0
Chicago (Central): 1
Denver (Mountain): 2
Los Angeles (Pacific): 3

key: COMP.DIG.L14.01|Look at the deadline. What time is the paper due in Baltimore? 5:00 PM, 4:00 PM, or 6:00 PM?
how: Watch how Aryeh handles a deadline. His paper is due 5:00 PM Central time. Central is 1 hour behind Eastern, so he adds 1 hour: 6:00 PM in Baltimore. He puts "Accounting paper due 6:00 PM" in his calendar with a reminder the day before.
pic: Course: Intro to Accounting (college in Chicago)\nPaper due: 5:00 PM Central time\nYou live in Baltimore (Eastern time)

key: COMP.DIG.L14.01|Look at the deadline. The quiz closes 9:00 PM Pacific. What time is that in Baltimore? 9:00 PM, 6:00 PM, or 12:00 midnight?
pic: Course: World History (college in Los Angeles)\nQuiz closes: 9:00 PM Pacific time\nYou live in Baltimore (Eastern time)

key: COMP.DIG.L14.01|The professor asks for a PDF. Why? A PDF is always much longer to read, a PDF looks the same on every computer, or a PDF adds bright colors to pages?
COMP.DIG.L14.01|Your paper is done in a document. How do you get a PDF? Rename the file to end in .pdf, download or save it as PDF, or print it out and scan it?
COMP.DIG.L14.01|When should the calendar remind you about a big paper? After it is due, one minute before, or a few days before?

COMP.DIG.L14.01|Put the steps for a new assignment in order. The cards say: Hand it in on the course site and check it uploaded., Put the deadline in your calendar in your own time., Read the assignment and the file type asked.

COMP.DIG.L14.01|Your online course in Los Angeles has a test Friday at 2:00 PM Pacific. Shabbos starts in Baltimore at 4:40 PM. Can you take it? Yes: it ends long before Shabbos; it does not matter what time it is; or no: it is 5:00 PM in Baltimore, after Shabbos starts?
pic:

key: COMP.DIG.L14.01|Look at the time zones. Which city is 3 hours behind New York? Los Angeles, Denver, or Chicago?
pic:
Time zones (hours behind New York)
New York (Eastern): 0
Chicago (Central): 1
Denver (Mountain): 2
Los Angeles (Pacific): 3

key: COMP.DIG.L14.01|What file type keeps your pages looking the same everywhere? PDF, a plain text file, or a photo of the screen?
COMP.DIG.L14.01|A Chicago course is due 11:00 AM Central. What time is that in Baltimore? 10:00 AM, 11:00 AM, or 12:00 noon?
pic:
Time zones (hours behind New York)
New York (Eastern): 0
Chicago (Central): 1
Denver (Mountain): 2
Los Angeles (Pacific): 3

key: COMP.DIG.L14.01|When it is 3:00 PM in Baltimore, what time is it in Chicago? 2:00 PM, 4:00 PM, or 3:00 PM?
how: A new way: time zones are like the sun rising across the country. It rises in Baltimore first, and an hour later in Chicago. So Chicago's clocks show an hour earlier than ours.

key: COMP.DIG.L14.01|In the simpler step, how many times do you write for each deadline? One, none, or two?
how: A simpler step: for every deadline, write two times in your calendar: the college's time and your own time.

key: COMP.DIG.L14.01|What from Long Documents do college papers need? Typing games to warm up, passwords for the course, or headings and footnotes?
how: The skill underneath: Long Documents (Computing Level 12). College papers need headings, page numbers and footnotes, and then a PDF to hand in.

key: COMP.DIG.L14.02|What does Shmuel share? His whole screen, every window; only the slides window; or his email inbox and his slides?
how: Watch how Shmuel shares his screen in a group project meeting. He closes his email first. He chooses "share a window" and picks only the slides window, not his whole screen. Everyone sees the slides and nothing else.

key: COMP.DIG.L14.02|You have a question while the professor is talking. What do you do? Type it in capital letters, unmute and interrupt him, or use the raise-hand button?
COMP.DIG.L14.02|You want to record a shiur on video to review later. What must you do first? Record it secretly without asking, ask the rebbe and the group, or record only the end of the shiur?
COMP.DIG.L14.02|Before a job interview on video, what should you check? Camera, microphone and a quiet, neat background; only that your shoes are shined well; or nothing; it will surely be fine?
COMP.DIG.L14.02|Which is safest when sharing your screen? Share only the window you need, share your email inbox and files, or share your whole screen at once?
COMP.DIG.L14.02|What must you do before recording a meeting? Turn off your camera, ask everyone, or nothing at all?
COMP.DIG.L14.02|In the classroom idea, what is like the mute button? Sitting in the very front row, staying quiet until called on, or leaving the room a little early?
how: A new way: a video class is like sitting in a real classroom. You would not shout from the back or walk in late; you raise your hand and speak when called on.

key: COMP.DIG.L14.02|Which Master Your Computer skill helps with screen sharing? Building spreadsheets, typing in Hebrew letters, or working with windows?
how: The skill underneath: Master Your Computer (Computing Level 10). Knowing your windows lets you share just the right one and switch back fast.

key: COMP.DIG.L14.03|Why do some apps ask for more than they need? They are broken and very confused, your information is worth money to them, or they are bored and just curious?
how: Apps and websites ask for permissions: your location, your contacts, your microphone. Many ask for more than they need, because your information is worth money to them. A careful adult reads before tapping "Allow". You will learn to check each request against what the app really does.

key: COMP.DIG.L14.03|Look at the siddur app. How many requests does Elazar allow? 2, 1, or 3?
how: Watch how Elazar checks his new siddur app. Location: it shows zmanim for his city, so it needs that. Storage: it saves his bookmarks, so it needs that. Contacts: no reason given, and a siddur does not need his friends' numbers. He allows two and says no to one.

Allow both of them right away without thinking; deny both of them and delete the whole app; or allow location if he wants nearby shuls, say no to contacts?
