key: COMP.DIG.L14.03|In the house idea, what is like a flashlight app asking for contacts? A plumber asking for your drawers, a plumber asking for the sink, or a guest saying hello?
how: A new way: an app asking for permissions is like a guest asking to see rooms in your house. A plumber needs the kitchen, not your bedroom drawers.

key: COMP.DIG.L14.03|What is the one habit? Read the request before tapping Allow, always tap Allow as fast as you can, or never install any apps at all?
how: A simpler step: one habit: never tap Allow without reading the request first.

key: COMP.DIG.L14.03|What did My Name Online teach? Keep your details private, type faster on the keyboard, or make graphs in a sheet?
how: The skill underneath: My Name Online (Computing Level 13). There you kept your details private. Permissions are the same idea: share only what is needed.

key: COMP.TYPE.L15.01|What does Typing Master ask for? 65 at 97 for 10 minutes, 80 at 90 for 1 minute, or 60 at 97 for 5 minutes?
how: This is the top of the typing ladder: 65 words a minute with 97 of every 100 words right, held for a full 10 minutes. Very few people reach it. It takes steady breathing, good posture and stamina, the same way a long shiur takes focus to the end. Reach it and typing will never hold your work back again.

key: COMP.TYPE.L15.01|Look at the test. How many words a minute? 132, 66, or 660?
how: The test is now 10 minutes, so divide by 10. 3,300 letters and spaces ÷ 5 = 660 words. 660 ÷ 10 minutes = 66 words a minute.
pic: Master test: 10 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 3300\nWords with a mistake: 18 of 660

key: COMP.TYPE.L15.01|Look at the test. Does it earn Typing Master? No, accuracy is too low; no, speed is too low; or yes, both reach the goal?
how: Watch how we judge the test. Speed 66. Mistakes 18 of 660, so 642 ÷ 660 = 0.973, about 97 out of 100. 66 is at least 65, and 97 is at least 97. He earns Typing Master.
pic: Master test: 10 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 3300\nWords with a mistake: 18 of 660

key: COMP.TYPE.L15.01|Look at this test. How many words a minute? 136, 34, or 68?
pic: Master test: 10 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 3400\nWords with a mistake: 34 of 680

key: COMP.TYPE.L15.01|Look at the same test. Does it earn Typing Master? Yes, it does; no, accuracy is too low; or no, speed is too low?
pic: Master test: 10 minutes\nLetters and spaces typed: 3400\nWords with a mistake: 34 of 680

key: COMP.TYPE.L15.01|In minute 8 your shoulders ache and you slow down. What helps most over 10 minutes? Good posture and steady breathing, holding your breath to focus, or hitting the keys much harder?
COMP.TYPE.L15.01|Which result earns Typing Master? 66 at 95 for 10 minutes, 70 at 98 for 5 minutes, or 67 at 98 for 10 minutes?
COMP.TYPE.L15.01|Put a stamina plan in order. The cards say: Add 2 minutes each week until you reach 10., Hold 65 for 4 minutes with no more than 3 mistakes., Take the full 10-minute test.

COMP.TYPE.L15.01|Your yeshiva's office needs someone to type up the whole year's minutes of meetings. You are a Typing Master. What should you tell them? That you type "okay", more or less; nothing; let them guess; or your speed, accuracy and the 10-minute certificate?
COMP.TYPE.L15.01|3,500 letters and spaces in 10 minutes. Words a minute? 35, 70, or 140?
COMP.TYPE.L15.01|700 words with 14 mistakes. Accuracy out of 100? 86, 98, or 96?
COMP.TYPE.L15.01|How long is the Typing Master test? 5 minutes, 2 minutes, or 10 minutes?
COMP.TYPE.L15.01|In the bike-ride idea, what wins a 10-minute test? Stopping halfway for a rest, staying steady to the end, or rushing hard at the start?
how: A new way: 10 minutes of typing is like a long bike ride. You keep one steady, calm pace from start to finish; you do not race at the start and run out of strength at the end.

key: COMP.TYPE.L15.01|In the simpler step, how long is the first run at 65? 2 minutes, 20 minutes, or 10 minutes?
how: A simpler step: hold 65 for 2 minutes. When you can, hold it for 4. Build up 2 minutes at a time.

key: COMP.TYPE.L15.01|What did Professional Typing ask for? 65 at 97 for 10 minutes, 60 at 97 for 5 minutes, or 50 at 96 for 5 minutes?
how: The skill underneath: Professional Typing (Computing Level 14). There you held 60 at 97 for 5 minutes. Typing Master adds 5 words a minute and doubles the time.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.01|Look at the speed test. How fast is the upload? 40, 4, or 10?
how: The router takes the internet that comes into the building and shares it by Wi-Fi. A speed test measures it in megabits per second: download is how fast things come to you, upload is how fast you send.
pic:
Speed test result
Download: 40 megabits per second
Upload: 10 megabits per second
A video call needs about 4 megabits per second each way.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.01|Look at the download. How many seconds will it take? 100, 20, or 3?
how: Watch how Dov works out a download time. The file is 100 megabytes. Each megabyte is 8 megabits, so it is 800 megabits. At 40 megabits per second, 800 ÷ 40 = 20 seconds.
pic: File to download: 100 megabytes\nConnection: 40 megabits per second\n1 megabyte = 8 megabits

key: COMP.DIG.L15.01|Look at the speed test. How many video calls could the upload handle at the same time? 1, 2, or 10?
pic:

A video call needs about 4 megabits per second each way.

COMP.DIG.L15.01|Only your laptop is offline; the phones work fine. Where is the problem likely? Your laptop, the router, or the whole street?

pic:

key: COMP.DIG.L15.01|What is the first step of Fix It Yourself? Buy a new router, call everyone you know, or read the message?
how: The skill underneath: Fix It Yourself (Computing Level 10). Network trouble uses the same routine: read the message, try one change at a time, write it down, then ask.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.02|Which jobs should the computer do for you? Jobs you do only once, jobs you repeat often, or jobs that need deep thinking?
how: If you do the same job by hand again and again, the computer can probably do it for you. A template starts every letter the same way. A rule sorts your email into folders by itself. Rename-many names a hundred files in one step. A student or worker who lets the computer do the dull jobs has more time for real thinking.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.02|Look at the rename. What is the name of the 7th file? Shiur 07, Shiur 7, or Shiur 70?
how: Rename-many uses a pattern. With the pattern "Shiur ##", the oldest file becomes Shiur 01, the next Shiur 02, and so on, always with two numbers.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.02|In the cookie idea, what is the template? The oven, the cookie cutter, or the topping?
how: A new way: a template is like a cookie cutter. You do not shape each cookie by hand; the cutter makes every one the same, and you just add the topping.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.02|In the simpler step, what do you make? Ten different rules, one template, or a brand-new computer?
how: A simpler step: make one template this week, for a letter you write often. Use it once.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.02|Which Level 11 tool changed many words at once? Find and replace, Ctrl+T for a new tab, or the long space bar?
how: The skill underneath: Shortcuts and Speed Tools (Computing Level 11). Find and replace was your first way of letting the computer change many things at once.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.03|Why must schoolwork you hand in be your own? AI is always right, honesty is a middah, or nobody ever checks?
how: AI tools can explain, summarize and draft, but they can be wrong, and work handed in as yours must really be yours. Honesty is a middah, not just a rule. You will learn when AI help is allowed, how to check what it says, how to say you used it, and why you never pass its work off as your own.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.03|You are not sure if AI is allowed on an essay. What do you do? Ask the teacher first, guess and hope, or use it quietly anyway?
how: First rule: use AI only where your rebbe or teacher allows it. Some assignments allow it for ideas; many do not allow it at all. When you are not sure, ask before you start.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.03|What did Moshe do with the quote he could not find? Made up a source, left it out, or used it anyway?
how: Watch how Moshe uses AI on an allowed research project. The AI says a scientist was born in 1867. He checks an encyclopedia: it agrees. The AI also gives a quote; he cannot find it anywhere, so he leaves it out. At the end he writes: "I used an AI tool to find first ideas; I checked every fact."

key: COMP.DIG.L15.03|An AI tool gives you a date for your history paper. What do you do? Ask the AI if it is sure, check it in a trusted source, or copy it straight into the paper?
COMP.DIG.L15.03|The teacher said "no AI" on this essay. A friend says nobody will know. What do you do? Let the friend write it, write it yourself, or use AI just a little?

COMP.DIG.L15.03|AI was allowed for ideas on your project. What do you add at the end? The AI's name written as the author, a note saying you used it and checked the facts, or nothing at all; it was allowed?
COMP.DIG.L15.03|Which job should you never give to AI? Finding first ideas when it is allowed, writing work you will hand in as your own, or explaining a hard word to you?
COMP.DIG.L15.03|Put the honest way to use AI in order. The cards say: Say that you used it., Ask if AI is allowed., Check every fact it gives in a trusted source.
COMP.DIG.L15.03|Never share private things with an AI tool. Which is private? Your address and family details, the name of a far planet, or a math question from class?
COMP.DIG.L15.03|Can AI tools be wrong? Yes, they can sound sure and still be wrong; only on Sundays, not other days; or no, they are never, ever wrong?
COMP.DIG.L15.03|Who decides if AI is allowed on an assignment? The AI tool itself, of course; your rebbe or teacher; or your friends in the class?
COMP.DIG.L15.03|What must you do with every fact an AI gives you? Delete it at once, trust it right away, or check it in a trusted source?
COMP.DIG.L15.03|In the chavrusa idea, what do you do before you say something is so? Just trust him, ask a third friend, or look inside yourself?
how: A new way: AI is like a chavrusa who reads fast but sometimes misremembers. You learn together, but you look inside the sefer yourself before you say something is so.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.03|What is the one rule? Never ask anyone questions, always use AI for everything, or never hand in AI writing as your own?
how: A simpler step: one rule: never hand in anything an AI wrote as your own.

key: COMP.DIG.L15.03|What did How AI Works teach? AI knows everything there is to know, AI predicts from patterns and can be wrong, or AI is a person who thinks like us?
how: The skill underneath: How AI Works (Computing Level 9). There you learned that AI predicts from patterns in data and can be wrong. That is why every answer must be checked.

key: COMP.DIG.L16.01|What makes a real computer expert? Patiently helping others learn, knowing more buttons than anyone else, or fixing it fast without saying a word?
how: The final level is about other people. A real computer expert is not the one who knows the most buttons; he is the one who can patiently help a younger boy, a rebbe or Zeidy fix a problem and learn to do it himself. Helping with patience and respect is a chesed. You will learn to listen, ask, show, let him do it, and write it down.

key: COMP.DIG.L16.01|Look at the call. What is the problem with Zeidy's tablet? The photos were never sent, the screen is broken, or the storage is full?
how: Start by listening, then ask one clear question: "What do you see on the screen?" The message on the screen usually tells you the problem.
pic: Zeidy: \"The tablet will not show the photos you sent.\"\nYou ask: \"What do you see on the screen?\"\nZeidy: \"It says: Storage full.\"

key: COMP.DIG.L16.01|Who taps the buttons in Chaim's help? Chaim grabs the tablet and does it, nobody taps anything at all, or Zeidy taps them himself?
how: Watch how Chaim helps Zeidy make room. He does not grab the tablet. He says: "Tap Settings. Now tap Storage. Do you see Old videos? Tap Delete." Zeidy taps each step himself. Then Chaim writes the three steps on a card, so Zeidy can do it again next month.

key: COMP.DIG.L16.01|Look at the call. What is Chaim's first question? Why did you ever do that to the tablet; did you break it, and how did that happen; or what do you see on the screen?
pic: Zeidy: \"The tablet will not show the photos you sent.\"\nYou ask: \"What do you see on the screen?\"\nZeidy: \"It says: Storage full.\"

key: COMP.DIG.L16.01|A younger boy cannot find his saved story. What is the best help? Tell him to go ask someone else, find it for him quietly and walk away, or show him how to search and let him try?
COMP.DIG.L16.01|After you fix a problem, what helps the person most next time? Only your phone number on a note, a short written list of the steps, or nothing; he will remember all of it?
COMP.DIG.L16.01|Your rebbe is frustrated that his slides will not show. How do you speak? Calmly and respectfully; quickly, with long technical words; or with a long, loud sigh first?
COMP.DIG.L16.01|Put the helping steps in order. The cards say: Write the steps down for next time., Listen and ask what the screen shows., Show one step at a time and let him do it.
COMP.DIG.L16.01|Why let the person tap the steps himself? So the whole thing takes much longer, so he learns to do it next time, or so you can rest your own hands?
COMP.DIG.L16.01|What is the first step when helping someone? Take the computer away from him and fix it alone; listen and ask what the screen shows; or restart it at once, before asking him anything?
COMP.DIG.L16.01|What is helping someone patiently with his computer? A way of showing off to others, a waste of good learning time, or a chesed?
COMP.DIG.L16.01|In the bike idea, what is like letting him tap the steps? Carrying the bike home for him, letting go of the seat, or riding the bike yourself while he watches?
how: A new way: helping with a computer is like teaching a younger boy to ride a bike. You do not ride it for him; you hold the seat, then let go, and he rides.

key: COMP.DIG.L16.01|What is the one sentence? "did you break it?", "give it to me", or "what do you see on the screen?"?
how: A simpler step: one sentence to remember: "What do you see on the screen?" Start every helping call with it.

key: COMP.DIG.L16.01|What routine from Fix It Yourself do you use when helping? Restart everything twice and wait; buy new parts for it right away; or read the message, one change at a time, write it down?
how: The skill underneath: Fix It Yourself (Computing Level 10). Helping someone uses the same routine: read the message, try one change at a time, write it down. Now you guide another person through it.

key: COMP.DIG.L16.02|What do you earn by finishing the capstone? A brand-new laptop of your own, the Computer Expert badge, or a whole day off from school?
how: This is your final project, the boss of the whole Computing ladder. You will plan, set up, secure and back up a computer for a shul office or a family business, and write a one-page guide so the person using it can manage alone. It brings together everything from Kindergarten to now. Finish it and you earn the Computer Expert badge.

key: COMP.DIG.L16.02|Look at the checklist. How many parts are still not done? 3, 2, or 1?
how: The project has five parts, in order: plan what the office needs, set up the computer, secure it, back it up, and write the guide. Check a part off only when it is really done.

key: COMP.DIG.L16.02|Which part is always last? The setup, the guide, or the plan?
COMP.DIG.L16.02|Who is the guide written for? Nobody in particular at all, other computer experts like you, or the person who will use the computer?
COMP.DIG.L16.02|In the sukkah idea, what is like the one-page guide? Putting up the four walls and the door, showing the family how to use it, or covering the top with plenty of schach?
how: A new way: the capstone is like building a sukkah for a family. You plan the size, put up the walls, make it sturdy, cover it with schach, and then show the family how to use it. Every part must be done before Yom Tov.

key: COMP.DIG.L16.02|In the simpler step, which part do you do first? Back up, Guide, or Plan?
how: A simpler step: do just the Plan part today. Write three things the office needs the computer for.

key: COMP.DIG.L16.02|What does the Set up part use from Level 13? Practice typing Hebrew words on the keyboard; power, Wi-Fi, sign in and updates; or video meeting manners and the mute button?
how: The skill underneath: Set Up a Computer (Computing Level 13). The Set up part of the capstone is exactly that lesson: power, Wi-Fi, sign in, updates, approved programs.

key: COMP.PROG.L10.01|Look at the code. What does it print? 5, 12, or 17?
how: Welcome to real Python. A variable is a labeled box that holds one value. Python keeps track of the kind of value in the box: a whole number, a decimal, text in quotes, or True and False. Knowing the kind tells you what + will do. This level makes you sure about every line you read.
pic: sefarim = 12\nsefarim = sefarim + 5\nprint(sefarim)

key: COMP.PROG.L10.03|In the worked example, why does the loop stop? The program runs out of lines; n becomes 5, and 5 <= 4 is False; or total reaches exactly ten?

n = 1
while n <= 4:
    total = total + n
    n = n + 1
print(total)

key: COMP.PROG.L12.02|Look at the edge test with exactly 10. What does the code print? True, 10, or False?
how: A test case is an input plus the answer you expect, written before you trust the code. Good programmers test normal inputs, edge inputs right on the line (like exactly 10 for a minyan), and strange inputs like an empty list. Tests catch mistakes before anyone depends on the program. Careful checking is part of doing a job honestly.

key: COMP.PROG.L12.02|Look at the three tests. Which test catches the bug? The test with 10, the test with 11, or the test with 9?
how: When a test prints something different from what you want, the test failed and the code has a bug. Compare each printed line with its "want" comment.
pic:
def is_minyan(n):
    return n > 10

print(is_minyan(9))     # want False

key: COMP.PROG.L14.03|In a queue, who is served first? The one who came first, whoever is tallest, or the one who came last?

key: COMP.PROG.L14.03|What does append do to a list? Removes the first item, sorts the list, or adds an item at the end?
how: The skill underneath: Lists in Depth (Computing Level 11). A stack is just a list where you only use append and pop at the end.

key: COMP.PROG.L15.01|Look at the division. Which error does it give? ValueError, ZeroDivisionError, or TypeError?
how: When Python cannot do a line, it stops with an exception, and its name tells you what went wrong: dividing by zero, a bad number, a missing place or key, or mixing text and numbers. Reading that name is the fastest way to fix a bug. A try and except block lets a program catch an expected problem and go on safely, instead of crashing in front of the user.
pic: print(10 / 0)

key: COMP.PROG.L15.01|Look at int("ten"). Which error does it give? IndexError, KeyError, or ValueError?
how: int("ten") fails because "ten" is text that does not look like a number. That is a ValueError: the right type, but a bad value.
pic: print(int(\"ten\"))

key: COMP.PROG.L15.01|In the worked example, why does the program not crash? Except ValueError catches the error, the print line is skipped, or int("abc") turns into a number just fine?
how: Worked example: int("abc") raises a ValueError inside try. Python jumps to except ValueError, which sets n to 0. The program does not crash; it prints 0 and goes on.

how: A simpler step: match the name to the problem. Zero under a division sign is always a ZeroDivisionError.

key: COMP.PROG.L15.01|Which is an edge test that might cause an exception? An empty list, a list with two names, or a normal list of five names?
how: The skill underneath: Test Cases (Computing Level 12). Edge tests, like an empty list or a zero, are exactly what cause exceptions. Testing finds them; try and except handle them.

key: COMP.PROG.L15.02|Look at math.sqrt(49). What does it print? 7, 7.0, or 24.5?
how: A library is a set of ready-made functions someone already wrote and tested. Instead of writing a square root from scratch, you import math and call math.sqrt. Real programmers reuse libraries all the time; the skill is reading what a function needs and what it gives back. Python also has built-in tools like sum, max, round and sorted.
pic: import math\nprint(math.sqrt(49))

key: COMP.PROG.L15.02|Look at math.floor(7.8). What does it print? 7, 7.8, or 8?
how: math.floor rounds DOWN to a whole number; math.ceil rounds UP. They are useful for counting whole things, like buses or tables.
pic: import math\nprint(math.floor(7.8))

key: COMP.PROG.L15.02|In the worked example, why use ceil and not floor? Ceil is shorter to type, floor only works on whole numbers, or you cannot leave boys without a seat?
how: Worked example: 25 boys, 10 seats per van. 25 / 10 is 2.5, but you cannot hire half a van. math.ceil rounds up, so the program says 3 vans.
pic:

boys = 25
seats = 10
print(math.ceil(boys / seats))

how: A simpler step: just read the name. math.floor goes down to the floor; math.ceil goes up to the ceiling.

key: COMP.PROG.L15.02|What do you give a function when you call it? A brand-new class to use; its return line from the end; or its inputs, in the brackets?
how: The skill underneath: Functions That Return (Computing Level 11). A library function is a function someone else wrote. You give it inputs and it returns an answer.

key: COMP.PROG.L15.03|Look at the three functions. What does the program print? Ari and Dov, Dov and Eli, or Ari and Dov and Eli?
how: Big programs are not written in one go. A good programmer first writes a plan: what the program must do, the parts it needs, what each part takes in and gives back, and the tests that prove it works. Then he builds one small part at a time. A chavrusa-pairing program, for example, has a part to load names, a part to make pairs, and a part to show them.

key: COMP.PROG.L15.03|Look at the pairing program again. Which part decides who goes with whom? Show, load_names, or make_pairs?
how: Each function owns one job and passes its result to the next. If something goes wrong, you know which part to look at.

COMP.PROG.L15.03|In that idea, what is like a function? The list of guests, one job given to one person, or the whole Shabbaton?
how: A new way: planning a program is like planning a Shabbaton. You list the jobs (food, rooms, schedule), give each job to one person, and check each job is done before Shabbos.

how: A simpler step: just split one task. "Make a learning schedule" can be split into: get the names, assign times, print the list.

key: COMP.PROG.L15.03|What does a reviewer look for in function names? That they clearly say what the function does, that they use only capital letters, or that they are as short as possible?
how: The skill underneath: Code Review (Computing Level 13). A good plan makes code that passes review: clear names, one job per function, and tests.

key: COMP.PROG.L16.01|Look at the map. How many places are one road from the Yeshiva? 3, 2, or 6?
how: A graph is a set of places joined by roads. Maps, train lines, and who-learns-with-whom are all graphs. In Python a graph can be a dictionary: each place is a key, and its value is the list of places one road away. With a queue, a program can search the graph ring by ring and find the fewest roads from one place to another, the way a map app finds a route.
pic:
roads = {
    "Home": ["Shul", "Bakery"],
    "Shul": ["Home", "Yeshiva"],
    "Bakery": ["Home", "Park"],
    "Yeshiva": ["Shul", "Park", "Library"],
    "Park": ["Bakery", "Yeshiva"],
    "Library": ["Yeshiva"],
}
print(len(roads["Yeshiva"]))

key: COMP.PROG.L16.01|Look at visit("Home"). Which place is visited last? Park, Library, or Yeshiva?
how: Breadth-first search (BFS) visits the start, then every place one road away, then every place two roads away, and so on. It uses a queue so places are visited in the order they were found.

key: COMP.PROG.L16.01|In the worked example, why does BFS give the fewest roads? It always picks the place with the shortest name; it tries every possible route there is and adds them all up; or it reaches every place ring by ring, nearest first?
how: Worked example: from Home to Library. Ring 1: Shul and Bakery (1 road). Ring 2: Yeshiva and Park (2 roads). Ring 3: Library (3 roads). The first time BFS reaches a place is always by the fewest roads.
